```{r setup, include=FALSE}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(dplyr); library(readr); library(knitr); library(kableExtra)})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
source("../06_appendix_sources/cite.R")   # numbered citations: cite("key")
col_spec <- function(...) if ("latex_valign" %in% names(formals(kableExtra::column_spec))) kableExtra::column_spec(..., latex_valign = "m") else kableExtra::column_spec(...)
styled <- function(df, align, widths, bold_first = TRUE, font_size = 8.5, caption = NULL) {
  k <- kable(df, format = "latex", booktabs = FALSE, align = align, escape = TRUE, caption = caption) %>%
    kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = font_size, full_width = FALSE, position = "center") %>%
    row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, color = "white", background = "#1f3350")
  n <- length(widths)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) k <- col_spec(k, i, width = paste0(widths[i], "cm"), bold = bold_first && i == 1,
                                         border_left = i == 1, border_right = i == n)
  k
}
tb <- function(...) tibble::tribble(...)

bt <- read_csv("../01_affordability/outputs/dgs10_backtest.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
model_order <- c("Random walk (no change)", "ARIMA(1,1,1)", "Damped trend (Holt)",
                 "Random walk with drift", "Linear trend (10y)")
b6  <- bt %>% filter(horizon_months == 6)  %>% select(model, mae6 = mae)
b12 <- bt %>% filter(horizon_months == 12) %>% select(model, mae12 = mae, rmse12 = rmse, ratio12 = mae_vs_rw)
btab <- left_join(b6, b12, by = "model") %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model, model_order)) %>% arrange(model) %>%
  transmute(Model = as.character(model),
            `MAE, 6m` = sprintf("%.2f", mae6), `MAE, 12m` = sprintf("%.2f", mae12),
            `RMSE, 12m` = sprintf("%.2f", rmse12), `MAE vs no change, 12m` = sprintf("%.2f", ratio12))
n_origins <- bt$origins[1]
```

All data are public and were downloaded November 9-11, 2026. Comparisons use each series' observation date, not the report date. Each driver folder holds the scripts, raw downloads, output CSVs and a verification log for every builder and release figure. Sources are listed on the final page.

## Driver 1: affordability and the rate range

**Affordability.** Payment = principal and interest on a 30-year fixed loan with 20% down, plus property tax at 0.90% of price and insurance at an assumed 0.50%, divided by median household income. October 2026 applies the October rate to the September median new-home price, with 2025 income carried forward. The 36.6% burden against 29.9% in 2018-19 is a national-median illustration; it tracks the Atlanta Fed HOAM index closely (correlation 0.87 in levels, 0.90 in 12-month changes), so the direction is the robust part.

**Rate range and scenarios.** The rate in h weeks is centered on the latest weekly reading, with the standard deviation of weekly changes over 1971-2026 scaled by the square root of h (normal errors, constant volatility). Upside is below 6.25% (about 12%), base 6.25-8.00% (about 73%, of which 6.75-7.50% is about 37%), downside above 8.00% (about 15%). The boundaries are reporting choices, and the weights describe the rate 52 weeks out, not the probability of the industry outcomes paired with each scenario. The full-history 80% range covered 82% of 12-month outcomes, against 66% for a two-year-volatility range (Exhibit A1.1).

A forecast that extends the recent trend in the 10-year Treasury yield missed by about `r sprintf("%.2f", bt$mae[bt$horizon_months == 12 & bt$model == "Linear trend (10y)"])` points on average at 12 months over 1990-2026, against `r sprintf("%.2f", bt$mae[bt$horizon_months == 12 & bt$model == "Random walk (no change)"])` for assuming no change. The rate range is therefore centered on today's rate.

**Rate drops and sales.** 12-month change in log new-home sales on the change in the mortgage rate and in unemployment. Since 2000 a 1-point rate drop goes with +5.6% sales (95% interval +1.9% to +9.4%, R-squared 0.05; +8.8% over 1976-2026); the six-month lag is not significant. The subsidy illustration is the present value of 84 months of payment savings at 6.00%, as a share of price -- not a builder's buydown cost.

## Driver 2: inventory

**Price cuts and supply.** Monthly OLS of the share of builders cutting prices on months' supply, Jul 2022-Sep 2026 (n = 49). Each month of finished supply goes with about 9.1 points more builders cutting (R-squared 0.42); total supply shows nothing. The result holds with lags and a rate control but not in first differences (p = 0.27), so it is a hypothesis to monitor, not a causal estimate (Exhibit A2.1).

**Finished-inventory outlook.** An identity, not a forecast: ending stock = beginning stock + homes entering finished inventory - finished homes sold, with inflow backed out of the last 12 months. From 111K, repeating last year's flows ends near 100K by September 2027; a smaller construction pipeline gives about 83K and weaker finished sales about 121K. These are not outputs of the rate scenarios.

## Driver 3: build costs

**Implied cost per home** = average selling price x (1 - gross margin); the seven-builder median change is +1.3%. Because it is derived from margin, "cost fell less than price" restates "margin fell"; the independent evidence is goods-input PPI (+8.7% y/y) and builder land commentary, used directionally.

**Margin arithmetic.** New margin = 1 - (1 - GM) x (1 + c) / (1 + p) for price change p and cost change c, holding mix constant. Each 1% of price or cost is about 80 bps; from 19.6%, price -1.0% and cost +0.5% give -122 bps.

## Driver 4: margins and starts

**Starts model.** 3-month-average starts = 35.5 + 0.647 x 3-month-average permits + 0.332 x lagged starts (K, SAAR), Apr 2018-Sep 2026, 102 months. Out of sample (33 target months), holding permits flat gives 6.9% MAPE at 12 months against 7.9% for no change; with actual permits it is 2.2%. The plotted band (±31K, about 63K wide) is model error given permits, which is why the 103K base-to-upside gap sits outside it; with permits held flat the equivalent is about ±130K. The model turns assumed permit paths into starts and does not forecast permits: shifting every forward permit input by 50K moves average starts by about 42-43K, so most of the scenario gap is the permit assumption.

## Limitations

- National medians are not matched new-home buyers; 2025 income is carried forward and insurance is assumed.
- Seven public builders are not the industry; quarters, margin definitions, incentives and impairment accounting differ.
- The rate range assumes a stable distribution of weekly changes; no joint rate, demand, permits or margin model is estimated.
- The price-cut relationship is correlational and does not survive first differencing; NAHB shares are not seasonally adjusted.
- The inventory outlook and starts paths are conditional on assumed flows and permits; long-horizon starts errors overlap (about three independent annual observations).
- Permit paths, margin ranges and monitoring thresholds are judgments.
